public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 341

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/341](https://www.erdosproblems.com/341)
* [Ben Green's Open Problem 7](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.1)
* [Li26] Li, Z., *Counterexamples to Erdős Problem 341* (2026),
  https://github.com/LiAlreadyExists/Erdos-341/blob/main/paper/Erdos341.pdf
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat Set Filter
open scoped Topology

namespace Erdos341

/--
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ be a finite set of integers and extend it to an infinite
sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n \geq k$ to be
the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i + a_j$ with $i,j \leq n$.
Is it true that the sequence of differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ is eventually periodic?

This problem is discussed under Problem 7 on Green's open problems list.

The answer is no: Li [Li26] (with GPT-5.6 Sol) showed that the greedy extension of the seed set
$A = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 22, 27, 28, 32, 36, 40, 47, 48, 52, 63, 71, 77, 81, 89, 97\}$ has a
sequence of differences that is not eventually periodic. The linked formal proof
exhibits such a sequence `a : ℕ → ℕ` (strictly increasing, with the greedy rule holding from
some index on, and with `n ↦ a (n + 1) - a n` not eventually periodic); casting it to `ℤ`
gives a counterexample to the statement below.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos341.lean#L12"]
theorem erdos_341 :
    answer(False) ↔
      ∀ (a : ℕ → ℤ),
        (∀ᶠ n in atTop,
          IsLeast { x | a n < x ∧ x ∉ { a i + a j | (i ≤ n) (j ≤ n) } } (a (n + 1))) →
        let d := fun i ↦ a (i + 1) - a i
        ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ m in atTop, d (m + p) = d m := by
  sorry

end Erdos341

reformulations.difference: Rather than explicitly specifying a finite increasing seed and its greedy extension, Lean quantifies over arbitrary integer-valued sequences satisfying the greedy rule eventually. It imposes neither global strict monotonicity nor positivity (the latter is used in Li's paper).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The eventual IsLeast condition forces an eventually strictly increasing, hence unbounded, integer tail. Choose a cutoff where the tail has passed every earlier value. Sorting and deduplicating the finite prefix, then appending the unchanged tail, produces a globally increasing sequence with the same prefix sets and forbidden sums thereafter. Its gaps differ only by finite reindexing, which preserves eventual periodicity. Non-positive initial entries can also be discarded: their sums with any previous entry cannot exceed the current maximum. Conversely, every finite-seed greedy extension satisfies the Lean hypothesis. Proved both universal-claim equivalences, with global strict monotonicity and with strict monotonicity plus positivity, as Review341.raw_iff_increasing and Review341.raw_iff_positive_seed in /workspace/review/normalization.lean, without using the sorry-backed problem theorem.
